the recent decline of the Arctic sea ice is likely to be caused by the combined effects of internal climate variability and anthropogenic forcing, and that the Arctic sea ice will probably recover to the level of previous years in the future.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
it is too early to make any predictions about a long-term trend of sea ice in the Arctic Ocean.

the observed decline of the Arctic sea ice is a consequence of the interaction between internal climate variability and external forcing, in particular, anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions and the resulting warming of the Arctic.
the Arctic sea- ice cover has been in a state of decline for at least two decades and is now in a state of extreme decline.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Arctic Ocean is not a passive receiver for the external climate forcing, but a dynamic and complex system with a rich internal variability that can be a source for further changes of the climate.
the observed thinning of the summer sea-ice extent since the 1990s is not necessarily a result of global warming, but is also a consequence of internal climate variability.
the Arctic summer sea ice cover is highly vulnerable to internal variability and the recent decline is not necessarily the sign of global warming.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a substantial decrease of summer sea-ice extent can occur even in the absence of a strong positive trend of the Arctic sea ice.

the observed recent decline of the Arctic sea ice can be regarded as the result of the superposition of two different signals: (1) the signal of the internal variability of climate, which has a strong interdecadal component, and (2) the signal of anthropogenic global warming.
internal climate variability is a crucial factor for the recent sea-ice decline.
